items.originalTitle: The Defenders of Mexico’s Scorpion Reef
items.author: Teresa Tomassoni
items.title: The Defenders of Mexico’s Scorpion Reef
items.summary: Climate change and illegal fishing are threatening the Gulf of Mexico’s largest coral reef. Inside the battle to protect it. By Teresa Tomassoni ABOARD THE MV SHARKWATER—At 5 a.m. on a Sunday in September, crew members aboard the MV Sharkwater, a ship operated by the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, readied a small inflatable motorboat tied alongside the larger vessel for a pre-dawn mission. The night before, the crew received a report about an illegal sport fishing boat anchored just off Isla Desterrada, a sandy islet inside the Alacranes Reef National Park, a federally protected area located about 70 miles off the northern coast of the Yucatán peninsula. At more than 1,300 square miles, the park includes the largest coral reef in the Gulf of Mexico. Images captured by a drone pilot for Sea Shepherd, an international marine conservation nonprofit, showed seven men from the boat setting up camp on the island. The crew was eager to confront them before they headed out to sea. “We want to catch them before they leave to go fishing,” said David Hance, Sea Shepherd’s director of operations, slipping on his lifejacket as he prepared to step onto the smaller vessel rocking in the dark early-morning swells. They would need to move fast, though, he said. Since the 1970s, Sea Shepherd has dispatched crews around the world to investigate, document and disrupt activities that jeopardize marine life. They run direct-action campaigns to stop industrial krill fishing in Antarctica, mass dolphin hunts in the Faroe Islands and poaching in the Upper Gulf of California. Combating illegal fishing inside Alacranes Reef National Park—commonly referred to as Scorpion Reef—is one of the organization’s newest initiatives aimed at helping Mexico safeguard some of its most prized marine protected areas where fishing and other potentially harmful activities are banned or highly regulated to safeguard important ecosystems like coral reefs.

items.title: Calls mount to shutter Osborn Correctional, one of CT’s oldest prisons
items.summary: OSBORN-1121 " data-image-caption=" Dallas Bailey sits at his station in the Waterbury barber shop where he works on December 18, 2025. " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_021-771x514.jpg" /> Dallas Bailey said his body hasn’t felt the same since the years he spent incarcerated at Osborn Correctional Institution. Roughly a year after arriving at the prison, Bailey reported significant gastrointestinal bleeding, medical records obtained by The Connecticut Mirror show. A physician recommended a colonoscopy or an at-home test, but it would take another 10 months — and a trip to the emergency room as the symptoms resurfaced — before he’d get the necessary testing. Doctors eventually diagnosed Bailey with an H. pylori infection, a bacterial stomach infection that can spread through contaminated food or water, among other avenues. Bailey believes he contracted the infection from Osborn’s drinking water, a claim also made by plaintiffs’ lawyers in an eventually settled 2016 class action against the state over conditions at the prison. “When you first get there, you realize, ‘Oh, this water is crazy.’ You can smell it. Then, after a while, you just have to drink the water,” Bailey said. “It’s sad, but you come to accept the fact that don’t nobody care.” Osborn is among the oldest Department of Correction facilities. People incarcerated there describe living conditions like discolored, foul-smelling drinking water, extreme heat and delayed medical care. Current and former officials say the prison is past its useful life. Supporters of efforts to close Osborn Correctional Institution held an October rally outside the Central Office of the state Department of Correction in Wethersfield. " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-771x514.jpg" src="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-771x514.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-1189559" srcset="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-771x514.jpg 771w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-336x224.jpg 336w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-768x512.jpg 768w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-1536x1024.jpg 1536w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-2048x1365.jpg 2048w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-1200x800.jpg 1200w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-1024x683.jpg 1024w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-2000x1333.jpg 2000w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-780x520.jpg 780w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OSBORN-RALLY-400x267.jpg 400w" sizes="(max-width: 771px) 100vw, 771px" /> Supporters of efforts to close Osborn Correctional Institution held an October rally outside the Central Office of the state Department of Correction in Wethersfield. Criminal justice reform organizers are now pushing for the state to shut it down. The “Close Osborn Coalition,” made up of multiple advocacy groups, plans to petition state officials for a phased-in closure of Osborn during the upcoming General Assembly session. The timing is strategic — an effort to capitalize on momentum from near-unanimous support for measures passed in 2026 to improve prison healthcare, said Alicia Strong, one of the organizers leading the effort. Strong also serves as co-director of the advocacy organization CT People’s Survival Programs. “This is not a place that anybody should live or work,” Strong said. “It seems like something that could bring a lot of different people who have a lot of different views about the prison system together under the banner of public health.” But the effort will face an uphill battle. DOC has no plans to close Osborn, according to spokesperson Andrius Banevicius. Even those who believe the prison should close say that doing so would require navigating a host of complicated logistics, including where to house the men currently incarcerated there. Closing a prison Osborn, located in Somers, is one of Connecticut’s oldest and largest prisons. Opened in 1963 as the Connecticut Correctional Institution-Somers, it originally served as the state’s maximum-security prison. In 1994, it was reorganized into a medium security institution and renamed Osborn Correctional Institution. Today, Osborn houses roughly 1,100 individuals, down from a peak population of over 2,000 between late 2007 and early 2008. The prison includes an inpatient medical hospital and one of the main hubs of the Correctional Enterprises of Connecticut, the state’s prison industry program that manufactures goods like clothing, furniture and signs. “The facility has run its course,” said Abraham Santiago, acting head of the Office of the Correction Ombuds, a state agency charged with overseeing DOC. “Department of Correction has buildings that have been closed that are in far better condition than Osborn.” Banevicius said DOC is “committed to maintaining the condition of all its facilities including the Osborn Correctional Institution, to ensure a safe and functional environment for staff and incarcerated individuals alike.” A $120 million infrastructure improvement project is currently underway to bring new energy efficient windows and doors to Osborn, Banevicius added. Santiago does not consider the major expenditure a mark of success. “You’re basically borrowing money and throwing it at a building that should have been closed decades ago,” Santiago said. “Imagine what $100 million would do for communities.” Closing a prison requires the coordination of several state agencies, including DOC, the Office of Policy and Management, as well as the governor’s office. Connecticut has closed a handful of facilities in the last decade, including Willard Correctional Institution in 2023 and Northern Correctional Institution in 2021. In both cases, the state cited the declining prison population and cost savings opportunities as reasons for closure. Criminal justice advocate Barbara Fair said that years of sustained organizing efforts helped to bring about the closure of Northern. Fair led the campaign, working with organizations like Yale Law School and regularly publishing op-eds, holding public hearings and hosting press conferences over the course of a “couple of years.” “Hopefully we won’t need that [long] with Osborn,” Fair said. Denise Paley sits in her home in Guilford on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. Paley serves as the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) Shoreline co-president. Paley serves as the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) Shoreline co-president. Credit: Connor Sharp / CT Mirror Denise Paley, whose son is incarcerated at Osborn, said she supports calls to close the prison but would like to see it done in such a way that doesn’t exacerbate issues at other facilities. “Osborn needs to close. It does,” Paley said. “But if they’re going to close Osborn and relocate everybody to another horrible facility, I don’t advocate for that.” Paley said that ideally she’d like to see a new facility built. As of now, the Close Osborn Coalition is proposing to reopen certain facilities previously closed by DOC that they believe are in better shape than Osborn, including Gates, Bergin and Enfield Correctional Institutions. Former DOC Commissioner Scott Semple said he doesn’t disagree that Osborn has outlived its usefulness, but reopening DOC’s shuttered facilities would require all kinds of fortification. And replacing a facility of Osborn’s size and complexity could cost the state upwards of $1 billion, he said. Prison labor Some people, like Santiago and Bailey, believe the effort to close Osborn will face additional challenges because of the goods produced by men working in its shops. The facility is one of the main production hubs for the Correctional Enterprises of Connecticut , or CEC, which produces furniture, chairs, laser engraving and clothing available for purchase by state agencies, municipalities, the federal government and certain nonprofit entities. “They’re never going to shut Osborn down,” Bailey said. “It makes too much money. That’s where the factories are.” OSBORN-1121 " data-image-caption=" Dallas Bailey at the Waterbury barber shop where he works on December 18, 2025. " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-771x514.jpg" src="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-771x514.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-1149445" srcset="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-771x514.jpg 771w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-336x224.jpg 336w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-768x512.jpg 768w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-1536x1025.jpg 1536w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-1200x800.jpg 1200w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-1024x683.jpg 1024w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-780x520.jpg 780w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032-400x267.jpg 400w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025_1218_SR_PrisonWater_032.jpg 2000w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 771px) 100vw, 771px" /> Dallas Bailey at the Waterbury barber shop where he works on Dec. 18, 2025. Credit: Shahrzad Rasekh / CT Mirror Roughly 200 men incarcerated at Osborn work making mattresses and clothing used by the correctional system. People incarcerated in Connecticut producing such goods make hourly wages of $0.90 to $1.50, according to a 2018 report by the Office of Legislative Research. “The real reason the state has been slow at closing down Osborn is because of the infrastructure in place. The 13th Amendment allows for a lot of this — the fact that we pay people slave wages to do this work,” Santiago said. DOC spokesperson Banevicius said the program provides incarcerated individuals with valuable vocational training, leading to better employment opportunities as they transition back to the community. Strong said she, too, has heard feedback that the jobs are important to the people who do them, and any plans to close Osborn would need to consider how to maintain those opportunities. Former DOC commissioner Semple said both points have some truth. “There is an argument that we use inmate labor to produce stuff at a low cost in terms of what they’re paid. But at the same time, you want some kind of structured activities and responsibilities,” he said. Public health concerns Public health concerns at Osborn are not new. Most recently, people formerly and currently incarcerated at the facility have voiced dissatisfaction with the water quality and episodes of extreme heat. Banevicius said the water is tested monthly by an independent contractor and consistently meets all applicable Connecticut Department of Public Health safety standards. A 2018 complaint filed against DOC in federal court by current and former individuals incarcerated at Osborn alleged they were exposed to toxic substances in several now-closed housing buildings and forced to drink and shower in contaminated water. The complaint described the facility’s water as “brown, cloudy or opaque, with a strong, acrid and offensive odor and taste” and alleged it caused skin rashes and gastrointestinal distress. It also alleged that at least 10 individuals had reported H. pylori infections while at Osborn, the same stomach infection Bailey contracted. But a plaintiffs’ expert said there was no accepted testing method to establish that Osborn’s water caused the infections. A plaintiff’s expert also tested the water and found it was potable and met all federal and state standards. The case settled in 2024, with the state paying $5,000 to each plaintiff without admitting liability, according to a settlement agreement provided by the state Attorney General’s office. But Bailey said the water issues were widely acknowledged during the four years he spent at Osborn — part of his eight-year sentence for assault and attempted robbery charges. Correctional officers bring their own water, and even therapy dogs drink bottled water, he said — a point also alleged in the 2018 complaint. “It’s not something that’s swept under the rug,” Bailey said of the water quality. “Everybody knows.” Bailey said his digestive issues have improved since his release from DOC custody in 2025, but he still experiences frequent stomach pain and sudden urges to use the bathroom immediately after eating. Correction Ombuds DeVaughn Ward testifies at a hearing of the Correction Advisory Committee in July 2026. Credit: Katy Golvala / CT Mirror Osborn is also one of just three DOC facilities that isn’t fully equipped with air conditioning, leading to sweltering temperatures during the summer months. A $25 million project is underway to install HVAC systems at Hartford and Bridgeport Correctional Centers, the other two facilities lacking AC. But the state does not have plans to bring facility-wide AC to Osborn. A January 2024 Department of Administrative Services feasibility study estimated that a “full facility retrofit” would cost between $76 million and $85 million. DOC estimated the actual project cost — including DAS fees, contingency fees and construction management — would be closer to $120 million. Instead, the state has spent $2.4 million over the last two years to bring 18 “industrial grade air conditioners” to Osborn, DOC spokesperson Banevicius said. Former Correction Ombuds DeVaughn Ward visited Osborn on July 1, during a multi-day heat wave that swept the East Coast. Using a temperature gun, Ward clocked a temperature of 85.6 degrees in the mess hall and kitchen. A cell in the C block registered a temperature of 81.5 degrees. The portable units DOC installed mostly provided cooling to the housing units, Ward said, but not in other areas, like the corridors, mess hall or kitchen. “Even though they’re pumping in AC, there are really questions about the efficacy of whether it’s really working in some housing units,” Ward said at the time. “I have long said, and I’ll continue to say, that [Osborn] is a facility beyond its useful life. That’s as a whole, not just with respect to the air conditioning.” One person incarcerated at Osborn wrote in testimony to the state’s Correction Advisory Committee in January that the extreme heat in the summer months makes him feel like he’s being suffocated. “The cell is so hot it literally feels like there is no air in the cell to breathe, throughout the night I have to constantly get up to drink water from my sink and wet a towel to lay across my stomach and chest in order to fall asleep for a few hours before my cellmate and I would have to repeat the process.” Paths to closure Organizers zeroed in on this moment to rally for Osborn’s closure in order to capitalize on momentum following legislative successes during the 2026 session, Strong said. A law passed nearly unanimously contained several measures related to prison healthcare reform, including the elimination of medical copays for people in DOC custody as well as the expansion of the correction ombuds’ health oversight capabilities. The Close Osborn Coalition is still gaining momentum. Organizers meet regulary and have hosted a few rallies. But it’s unclear whether organizers can build a sustained campaign that could ultimately lead to the prison’s closure. Mike Lawlor, professor of criminal justice at the University of New Haven and former House chair of the state Judiciary Committee from 1997 to 2011, said closing Osborn would not be easy. “Is Osborn a facility that really should be shut down based on the facility? Yes. Is there a way to actually do it? Maybe, but it’s complicated,” he said. Lawlor expects advocates will raise proposals this session that could decrease the overall DOC population, which could make space for people currently residing at Osborn. These include bail reform, which could reduce the pretrial DOC population, and parole eligibility for people who committed crimes when they were young. items.originalTitle: 'Not here to dilly-dally': Inside Teresa Benitez-Thompson's first trip to D.C. as Rep.-elect
items.author: Mini Racker
items.title: 'Not here to dilly-dally': Inside Teresa Benitez-Thompson's first trip to D.C. as Rep.-elect
items.summary: Just four days after Teresa Benitez-Thompson's (D-NV) historic victory , the congresswoman-elect touched down at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. Becoming a member of Congress is like joining a very old, very elite university — there's even a 10-day freshman orientation. Benitez-Thompson stayed with more than 100 other lawmakers who attended New Member Orientation at a hotel a few blocks from the Capitol. Police cars stood guard day and night. For nearly two weeks, the roughly $170-per-night property may have been the most exclusive in Washington. It was booked out for lawmakers, their spouses and two aides apiece. The next day, buses ferried the new members through security to the Capitol's historic steps for their first visit to the House floor. Many disembarked into the bright, crisp day looking a little lost. Not Benitez-Thompson. She brushed her hair off her face, stepped outside and immediately grinned at the camera. Benitez-Thompson has an impressive résumé that includes former Assembly Majority leader and chief of staff to Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford (D), the state's incoming governor. But it was her long-ago tenure as Miss Nevada that shone in those first moments on the Hill. How does it feel to be congresswoman-elect? "It's very cool," Benitez-Thompson told The Nevada Independent in a later interview. "There are moments where I feel absolutely overwhelmed, but like in a phenomenally good way, just taking in the history of the Capitol, walking into the chamber of the House floor for the first time, knowing the amount of history that's taken place there." The first Democrat ever to represent Northern Nevada's 2nd Congressional District is also the Nevada delegation's first new member in nearly a decade. The next one could arrive faster. Potential challengers are already eyeing the district, which was considered safely Republican before current Rep. Mark Amodei (R-NV) announced his retirement this year. In two years, some lucky GOP freshman may find themselves at their own orientation. Benitez-Thompson is determined to maximize the time she's got. Enjoying the present moment is her husband, KOLO chief meteorologist Jeff Thompson, who joined her for her first week in town, following her from the bus, taking photos of her on the Capitol steps, and snapping selfies together in front of the dome. After she'd won, she didn't know if he'd be able to come, since she only got the details about the trip the night after the election. "I wasn't exactly sure what the logistics were … because they only send them to you after The Associated Press calls your race," she said. "He told me that … he'd done his own research and figured out what New Member Orientation looked like, and he's like, 'I already got it off a month ago,' and I was like, 'What?!' He said he didn't want to tell me because he was worried it would freak me out too much." Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-NV) and her husband, Jeff Thompson, enter the United States Capitol for her first tour of the House floor on Nov. 8, 2026. (Mini Racker/The Nevada Independent) 'Kind of like kindergarten' Her preparation began before she left Reno. After she won, she had breakfast with Amodei. It wasn't their first meeting — they had a previously unreported lunch soon after the June primary at Benitez-Thompson's request. Back then, they talked about his 15 years in Congress and his perspective on rural parts of the district. She did not request his endorsement. This month, they met at Josef's, a longstanding Reno bakery. He gave her his cellphone number and named a few staffers she might consider "that were apolitical." To Amodei, the social dynamics of becoming a congressperson are pretty basic. "It's kind of like kindergarten," he said. "Treat people the way you wish you were treated." Benitez-Thompson said their meeting went "great." "I like it that he's kind of ending this note, being the Mark that we all know, our Carson City guy," she said. "He was committed to having continuity for the constituents he's helping, so he's going to make sure I get that casework information. … That's really, really kind and I do not take that for granted, because there are a number of members here who are getting zero information from their existing congressperson." In the packed days before orientation, Benitez-Thompson's aides, more used to a jeans-friendly Northern Nevada style, stocked up on Macy's suits. Once the Rep.-elect arrived in Washington, Rep. Dina Titus (D-NV), the delegation's dean, introduced Benitez-Thompson to the incoming Democratic caucus that now boasts more than 250 members. "I've known her for a long time and think the world of her, and so it was a treat to get to introduce her," Titus told The Nevada Independent . "There was a lot of excitement in the room. They just were so excited that Nevada had a whole blue sweep and that she was part of it and made history in doing so." Throughout orientation, placards directed the new lawmakers through the labyrinthine halls of the Capitol and the surrounding House office buildings. They attended the sort of briefings familiar to anyone starting a new job, on subjects such as payroll and benefits, hiring and security. "The thing that you sort of have to learn for yourself a little bit is what's the best use of your time," said Rep. Susie Lee (D-NV), who in 2019 was the most recent Nevada member sworn into the House. "When you're a new member, everything seems urgent and everything seems important." Many members don't get their district offices running until February, since they can't access funding before they are sworn in. Benitez-Thompson, however, is working to open her district office ASAP. Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-NV) tours House office buildings with aides in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 15, 2026. (Mini Racker/The Nevada Independent) Benitez-Thompson's time in Washington also included numerous political events. She attended receptions with the New Democrat Coalition, the largest House Democratic caucus, which describes itself as "center-left." She appeared at a celebration with Defend the Vote and a press conference with BOLD PAC, the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus. She also talked to national media outlets . Right before Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) name-dropped her in The Wall Street Journal, she told Politico that she had taken "a number" of congratulatory calls from likely presidential contenders. As with most potentially contentious national topics, she quickly steered the conversation back home, saying, "I'll be talking to any and everyone who can help me move resources." "She comes in as a star already," Titus said. "People who have met her have told me how much they like her, how she's so energetic. She's got experience from her legislative leadership role. She doesn't have to work very hard to make herself known." Benitez-Thompson, who built relationships across party lines in Carson City, is so far continuing that approach in Washington. "At least for the outset of these first couple weeks, there's a lot of camaraderie among the freshmen, regardless of ideology or partisanship," she said. "Everyone's talking to everyone. Everyone's shaking hands. Everyone's having introductory conversations." Titus said she wanted to encourage Benitez-Thompson by focusing on the positive, especially what they can work on together around affordability and environmental issues. But if there's one thing she learned since she first came to Congress, it's that the friendly faces don't always stay that way. "Maybe I learned that it's every man for himself," Titus said. "They say it's a system of relationships, but when it comes right down to it, it's really not, because everybody's got their own agenda and their own ambitions." Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-NV) and aides Nate Helton and Riley Sutton chat with Rep.-elect Chris Rabb (D-PA) in a House office building in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 15, 2026. (Mini Racker/The Nevada Independent) Trading spaces Another highlight of Benitez-Thompson's trip was the Library of Congress. "I love the smell of a library," she said. "It was pin-quiet in there, which when you're walking around in the constant echo chamber of marbled halls, the quietness of the library was just beautiful." Not every activity was so picturesque. A week after her floor visit, she toured the House office buildings to help decide which suite to select as her own. The first option, a gleaming, four-room-plus-bathroom space inside Cannon House Office Building, was unfurnished, but roomy, bright and full of potential. The offerings deteriorated from there. Many lawmakers seemed to have abandoned their offices in a hurry, leaving stained carpets and bits of paper and wires strewn across the floor. Benitez-Thompson appraised it all, running her hand over dusty mantels, opening cabinets and testing locked drawers. In one room, she peered into a rectangular hole in the wall that revealed metal pipes. In another, she tossed a piece of litter in the trash can, then arranged an abandoned pair of shoes neatly beside the bin, barely making a dent in the detritus. In the hallways, she peeked between the locked doors of the Ways & Means Committee room. When she happened upon former Speaker Nancy Pelosi's (D-CA) office, she stopped, but hurried on too quickly for The Nevada Independent to take a clear photo. Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-NV) picks up discarded shoes left in an abandoned House office in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 15, 2026. (Mini Racker/The Nevada Independent) The next day, Benitez-Thompson went out with Lee for drinks. The congresswoman had cabernet, the congresswoman-elect, an old fashioned. They talked strategy. Lee, House Democrats' current Battleground Leadership representative, previously held Benitez-Thompson's title as the most vulnerable Nevada Democrat in Congress. Ahead of 2028, Republicans are already sending press releases targeting both of them. "Being in what will be a frontline-of-the- Frontline district that she flipped, I told her it's most important for her to make sure she's back in the district as much as possible," Lee said. "There's things you can do that are not legislative that really demonstrate to your constituents that you're there to work with anyone. You know, making sure that you're setting up a good constituent service operation." Amodei agreed, saying his office's constituent services "served us well, and explained why we had the success we had when it came time for that every-two-year personnel session at the ballot box. But I think with Teresa's background, I sense that she is very well-read into that, social worker, hospice background, as well as the political stuff. … I'm sure that will be something that she understands from the get-go." Benitez-Thompson said she's also "highly focused on constituent services." And though Lee mentioned "literally running a re-election campaign right away," the Rep.-elect wouldn't yet say whether she'll run again, either. "I don't want to run for the sake of running," Benitez-Thompson said. "I want to run because I know that I'm doing the right kind of work for people, and so as long as I feel like I'm in that place where I'm doing that work, then I'll keep running, but I don't want to just say I'm going to run for the sake of running. I'm not living my life just to be a candidate on the ballot." Lee and Benitez-Thompson also discussed setting up her franking program to help communicate with constituents and strategized about what committees she might request. Lee gave her a "huge spreadsheet" showing what vacancies might be available. Lee's view is that Armed Services, Natural Resources or Agriculture committees could all be good fits, as would opportunities to work on healthcare. Amodei — who said being on committees connected to the district was "a phenomenally important part" of his first term in Congress — named mining, agriculture and tech as key issues. Benitez-Thompson wasn't yet ready to share her committee requests. Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-NV) selects her office in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 17, 2026. (Suzannah Hoover/The Nevada Independent) Nevada's senators have been in touch. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV) told The Nevada Independent Benitez-Thompson "was everywhere" when she was home in October, "particularly rural communities." Sen. Jacky Rosen (D-NV) said they have been talking "over the phone all the way through the campaign." Rosen has offered the congresswoman-elect a few tips. "I told her some of my friends in the House, like finding a place to live, if you need a roommate," Rosen said. "Trying to help how you schedule your hearings, because you're running maybe from Rayburn to Cannon, back and forth … Number one advice: Wear the comfortable shoes." Though the women in the delegation doubt Benitez-Thompson will need much from them, they're ready to help. "She's going to be a top priority because she's in a top district," Lee said. "We want to keep the seat blue, and I think she is a great person for that district, and I think she has a great chance of holding on to that seat. And we just need to do whatever we can to make her as successful as possible." 'Not here to dilly-dally' A hidden corridor of the Capitol Visitor Center hosts the last big event of New Member Orientation: the freshman room lottery. Benitez-Thompson got 18th pick. When her name was called at 10:55, she had five minutes to make final deliberations, settling on a first floor office in Cannon. Finally, she took her official portrait, an America 250 brooch from Elko's Northeastern Nevada Museum pinned to her lapel. The next day, House Democrats resoundingly — and anonymously — nominated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) for speaker. Jeffries hoped to speak with every new House Democrat before the vote. Benitez-Thompson declined to say whether they had met. "Right now, he's running uncontested," she said on Tuesday. "If someone else pops up, I'm going to look them in the eye, and the same thing: 'Here's what I'm trying to get done for Nevada. I've got two years to get this stuff done. There's a sense of urgency here. I'm not here to dilly-dally. You need to tell me how you're going to get us closer to that mark in the next two years.'" Her kids are excited to join her when she is sworn in on Jan. 3. They have a list of Washington activities, including a tour of the Capitol dome, to add to her calendar. She'll also spend hours traveling. There are no direct flights between Washington and Reno, but she told the Reno Gazette-Journal that she'll have an apartment in D.C. and return home on weekends. "I'm going to be ragged tired, but I'm going to do it," she told The Nevada Independent . "I'm going to be a super commuter. There are working moms out there who have it much worse. There are moms who are taking the bus one or two hours a day, working more than one job. I have no complaints." On Wednesday, Benitez-Thompson chatted with Lee and other members about how to make good use of her time in the car on trips across the district. "She was cute, because she said that given her beauty queen experience, that she knows a lot of people in all these districts because she was always going to these little towns doing all these beauty pageants," Lee said. "Now all these women she competed with are moms, so, leveraging those relationships as well. But I think she's going to be a great member. I think she has a level head and is ready to hit the ground running." More than ready. "As I meet with the new freshmen and talk with the new freshmen, we are all in the same place of, 'We want to get working now,'" Benitez-Thompson said. "There's a lot of us like myself who are coming in from seats that we won and that we don't take for granted. We're not here to play the long game. We're here to get stuff done right now in the two years that we know that we have." Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-NV) tours House offices in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 15, 2026. (Mini Racker/The Nevada Independent)

items.originalTitle: Home for the holidays? Maybe not this year
items.author: Jim Cameron | Columnist
items.title: Home for the holidays? Maybe not this year
items.summary: Price at the Cumberland Farms station in Storrs on May 1, 2026. Prices are slightly lower as Thanksgiving approaches. " data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/gasoline-5-1-26-3.jpg" /> Heading home for the holidays next week? Maybe not. For the first time in years, Thanksgiving travel won’t set a record. Mom’s turkey is still free. Getting to it is not. The culprit? Higher fuel prices . use this one " data-image-caption="" data-large-file="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/jim-cameron-talking-combo-1.jpg" src="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/jim-cameron-talking-combo-1-336x93.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-953193" srcset="https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/jim-cameron-talking-combo-1-336x93.jpg 336w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/jim-cameron-talking-combo-1-400x111.jpg 400w, https://ctmirror.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/jim-cameron-talking-combo-1.jpg 458w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 336px) 100vw, 336px" /> Gasoline prices are up… way up. An average gallon in Connecticut cost $3.94 last week , down a bit from the $4.30 we were paying a month ago, but still up 27% over last Thanksgiving. And domestic airfares are also soaring… by one estimate , up 31% over last year. And that’s for a middle-seat and $50 bag fee (thanks, JetBlue). And we all know how much fun (and how unreliable) our airlines have been of late, suffering under FAA ground halts and tech-woes. Frankly, I’ve always wondered why Americans spend so much money for so little vacation time at Thanksgiving, basically a four-day long weekend with hugely concentrated travel on Wednesday and Sunday. We pay peak prices to spend 30 hours in transit for 48 hours of family time to argue about politics and then head home. But if you can’t afford to drive or fly and you really want to get to Mom’s, there are options. Just don’t take them for granted without pre-planning. AMTRAK: Here in the Northeast Amtrak trains are also expensive and with limited, if slightly increased, capacity. And Thanksgiving week is the busiest all year for the railroad. Last year’s Thanksgiving ridership was 1.2 million, up nearly 6% over 2024. This year Amtrak is adding two extra round trips… but just between Washington and New York. Up here, we’ll get a few extra cars tacked on to their already busy trains. On a typical Wednesday a ride from Stamford to Boston costs as little as $39 (coach) one way. But the same trains on Wednesday November 25 cost $260 (also in coach). Ouch! That’s less a fare than a ransom note with pricey AmFood. And it’s all about supply (limited) and demand (stretched). Except for the uber-costly Acela, Amtrak trains between Washington and Boston offer reserved (but unassigned) seating. So don’t expect to stroll to the station and climb onboard without a ticket. And unless you paid extra for a Flex fare , your ticket can’t be changed to a different train. HARTFORD LINE: Here you’ll find both Amtrak and CTrail trains, so check your timetable. Some of the Amtrak trains are all-reserved (like the Vermonter) but others are first-come, first-served. CTrail honors all tickets but holiday ridership can lead to standing-room-only conditions. Confusing, right? That’s two railroads, one track, three sets of rules and minimal signs at the station explaining any of it. Welcome to Connecticut visitors! METRO-NORTH: Extra trains will be added but others dropped. Grab a magnifying glass and study this timetable closely as it’s confusing even to this veteran rider. The TrainTime app is a better choice for planning your journey. Of course there are no reservations on Metro-North, so it’s something of a free-for-all. Kind of like Black Friday at Walmart, with baggage. Metro-North’s busiest day of the year is the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, and it’s the one day of the holiday stretch when you will still get charged peak fares. Always buy (and activate) your e-ticket before boarding or your holiday travels will be soured with an on-board penalty, up to $8. Seniors can catch a break as they can buy tickets onboard without a penalty. Finally, a perk for getting old. My advice? Book now, pay up, pack light and lower your expectations. Or do what smart families do: let the kids come to you. More Zoom stuffing anyone?

items.title: Sephora’s CEO initially turned down an entry-level job at the company because she could only wear black, white, or gray to the office
items.summary: In 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That company was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its CEO. Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.” But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes. Patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand , which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco. “I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she said, well there is this company called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.” “Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I said, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.” “And I said, I’ll take the cigarette job.” Patrick, who emigrated to the U.S. from Iran at the age of 7, said her decision to take the DFS role rather than the beauty job wasn’t necessarily down to independence but rather to personal finances. After all, Patrick was a student, and her wardrobe was full of patterned dresses—she couldn’t afford to repurchase multiple monochromatic looks. DFS turned out to be an “incredible opportunity” that took Patrick around the world and quickly propelled her from the cigarette category into wine. But in 2006, Sephora came calling again courtesy of a referral from Carolyn Bojanowski, now Sephora’s executive vice president for merchandising. Patrick interviewed with the same HR representative she had turned down years before, and the corporate dress code of black, white, and gray (“concept colors,” as they were referred to at the time) was still in place. “They’d added red to the concept at that point,” Patrick recalls. “It was actually another, I think, six or seven years before we added color.” Building diverse teams Patrick’s path to Sephora and then up its ranks wasn’t linear—after DFS she worked at Restoration Hardware and Peet’s Coffee & Tea—and said this diversity of experience is now precisely what she looks for when building her own teams. “I feel that my job is to remove obstacles and to make sure that they get to do what we hired them to do,” added Patrick. “So I definitely believe in building diverse teams, and I do feel that my job as a leader is to protect them from the noise and deal with the things that I should be dealing with.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: What's behind Nevada's K-12 funding crisis, and how can it be fixed?
items.author: Rocío Hernández
items.title: What's behind Nevada's K-12 funding crisis, and how can it be fixed?
items.summary: As an alum of the Title I elementary school where she now teaches, Howard Wasden Elementary, Cristal Porter is deeply committed to supporting her students. But last school year, she was at risk of losing her position because of budget cuts driven by lower state funding due to enrollment declines. While her principal ultimately found a way to save her position, others weren't as lucky. "When I think of those displaced, surplused or forced into retirement last spring, I can only say what an infuriating and immeasurable loss for the students who need their dedication the most," Porter said at a Sept. 28 press conference to announce an emergency regulation to prevent a similar situation at the Clark County School District (CCSD) this year. When lawmakers adopted the state's K-12 education funding formula in 2019, their intent was to allow state funding to follow the student to whatever public school they choose, be it a district school or a charter school. The new funding model worked well when school districts were experiencing enrollment growth, but not so much today. School district and state officials are proposing adjustments to the formula that could provide more funding stability for school districts experiencing enrollment declines while continuing to work well for schools that are still growing. "Everybody's trying to do a good thing, trying to make this less volatile for districts and charter schools," said Melissa Willis, the state education funding manager for the Nevada Department of Education (NDE). But the decision on whether to tweak the formula will come down to lawmakers and Gov.-elect Aaron Ford (D) during the 2027 legislative session. Ford did not respond to a request for comment on the proposals. If these proposals go through, it would be the biggest alteration to the formula since it was implemented. "Changing and improving the way that schools educate kids is a very slow-moving process, and it takes several years," said Megan Griffard, an assistant professor of educational policy at UNLV. "Being able to stabilize the funding is really important because if things are just constantly changing, the improvements that we want to see don't happen." State Superintendent of Public Instruction Victor Wakefield explains a recent emergency regulation on K-12 education funding during a press conference at Howard Wasden Elementary School in Las Vegas on Sept. 28, 2026. (Rocio Hernandez/The Nevada Independent) How does student enrollment influence school funding? The idea behind the state's per-pupil funding model was to allow funding to follow the student. To ensure that, the state divides schools' funding into quarterly payments that are based on their students' average daily enrollment , which is calculated by dividing the number of days a student was enrolled in the previous quarter by the number of days in that quarter. This can result in funding fluctuations throughout the school year as new students enter the system or leave for a variety of reasons, including alternative schooling options or relocating to a different state. School systems start the year with a budget based on their enrollment in the fourth quarter of the previous school year. It's then adjusted quarterly. That means school districts experiencing declining enrollment don't feel the hit until the second quarter of the school year. CCSD noted in a Sept. 18 briefing that this wasn't as much of an issue when Nevada school districts were growing rapidly. It even helped them hire more teachers each fall. But during this period of enrollment dips, it's doing more harm than good. In addition to this, Willis said at the end of each quarter, schools must certify their average daily enrollment and report it to the department that audits the figure, a process known as true up. Willis said school districts may end up being owed funding or owing the state money if their figures are off. "If you're growing in enrollment, that's a great thing. Everybody wants more money," she said. "But if you're declining in enrollment, you're already having some budget challenges, having a lump sum that you're paying back every three months can be challenging." School districts spend months building their budgets with projected enrollment figures for their next school year. CCSD Chief Financial Officer Justin Dayhoff said if projected enrollment is off by even 2 percent, that could spell trouble for its budget when their funding is adjusted after the school year has already begun. That's what happened to Clark County schools this year. In September, the district announced its enrollment declined by more students than it projected and was on the verge of cutting its funding by about $50 million, prompting fears of staff layoffs. Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) stepped in and approved emergency funding to get school districts by until the start of the next legislative session. He made it clear that a more permanent plan was still needed. Daniela Gutierrez, right, observes as Joy Ammogawen teaches in her third grade classroom at Raul P. Elizondo Elementary School in Las Vegas on November 21, 2025. (Daniel Clark/The Nevada Independent) Clark County schools' plan Instead of tying per-pupil funding to quarterly enrollment averages, the Clark County School District is is working on a bill draft request that would tie it to how many students were enrolled on a single day from the previous school year, Oct. 1, or "the percentage increase in that enrollment on October 1 over the immediately preceding 3 school years," whichever is greater. "It addresses schools or for charters who are increasing in enrollment," he said. "It's your Oct. 1, but also every year you're going up 100 students, so it's your Oct. 1 plus 100 kids, for example." He said the state already uses enrollment data from that date to calculate additional funding for students who fall into speciality categories — at risk of not graduating, gifted and talented, or learning English as a second language — so this change would bring both funding blocks into alignment. "At the end of the day, this isn't about avoiding the inevitable," he said during an Oct. 29 interview. "If we're in declining enrollment, we still have to address that, but what it would allow us to do would be to address that in the spring rather than the fall." The Commission on School Funding, a state panel of school funding experts created by the Legislature, is planning to recommend a similar approach in its bill draft request. During the commission's Oct. 23 meeting, several members, including charter school officials, said they thought it was the simplest way to address school districts' budget crisis. The commission's chair, Guy Hobbs, said using the Oct. 1 date would be beneficial for school districts for the foreseeable future as enrollment is expected to keep declining. A recent report by the Guinn Center for Policy Priorities, a local nonpartisan think tank, projected Nevada public schools would experience a 1.6 percent decrease in enrollment between 2023 and 2031, but it may reach that level sooner. Exterior sign at the State of Nevada Department of Education offices on Wednesday, June 14, 2023. (Jeff Scheid/The Nevada Independent) Education department's plan The state education department is considering proposing a different approach. Willis said the department would prefer to use enrollment figures that are as current as possible and that can work for all school system types, whether they are growing or declining. Willis said the department has been exploring using a four-quarter enrollment average but going off a calendar year instead of a fiscal year. Under this proposal, funding for the 2027-28 school year would be based on the 2026 four-quarter average, which would make the data available when school districts typically build their budgets. Willis said this is a good middle ground solution because enrollment tends to be higher at school districts in the first half of their school year but trickles down during the second half, while the opposite tends to happen at charter schools. Under this proposal, the state will no longer require certification and audit of schools' enrollment at the end of each quarter, Willis said. Willis said this will allow school districts to build out their budgets with confidence, knowing their per-pupil funding "is not going to change even if their enrollment starts to drop." In order to avoid funding issues for schools still experiencing growth under either proposal, the commission and education department are proposing expanding another mechanism in the funding model, the Exceptional Enrollment Growth Adjustment. Willis said right now, this adjustment is mainly available for charter schools experiencing enrollment growth of 25 percent or more. This allows them to receive more funding before the beginning of the school year. The education department and the commission are recommending the Legislature lower the eligibility threshold to 15 percent. They are also proposing to make this adjustment available to all qualifying school types, or any school that is opening or adding a grade level regardless of whether they meet the 15 percent threshold. "Whatever method is used needs to be able to work in the long run for an enrollment declining environment and an enrollment growing environment, or an environment where some of the districts are growing and some are declining," Hobbs said. Other ideas The Guinn Center has a different approach. Nevada's funding formula provides additional per-pupil funding, known as weighted funding, for students with extra needs, such as English language learners, students who are gifted and talented, and students who are at risk of not graduating. Students that need special education also get separate additional funding. Students who fit multiple categories are only funded for their highest applicable weight. The Guinn Center's recent report suggests the state uses this moment of declining enrollment to open up more weighted funding to students that fit more than one of these categories. Hobbs said the commission is concerned that if the state funds students for multiple weights, it could risk all students' receiving smaller per-pupil funding allocations if more of the funds have to be dedicated to serving certain populations. The commission suggests the state wait to implement this policy until the gap between Nevada's per-pupil funding average and the national average is 90 percent closed. The commission is also looking at adjusting the funding formula's hold-harmless provision for school districts where enrollment declines by 5 percent or more. The provision allows those school districts to be funded at their enrollment level from the previous school year. The commission is proposing lowering that threshold to between 3 percent and 4 percent to make it easier for districts to reach that trigger. The Guinn Center's report says temporary hold-harmless policies may give school districts time to adjust to the enrollment shifts, but it warns against permanent hold-harmless policies that "would subsidize districts for students that they are ultimately no longer serving."
